Old Goa (Konkani: Pornnem Goem, Adlem Gõi, Goeam; ) is a historical city situated on the southern banks of the Mandovi River in the Ilhas (present-day Tiswadi) sub-district of North Goa in the Indian state of Goa.

The city was established by the Bijapur Sultanate in the 15th century, following the Portuguese conquest of Goa it served as capital of Portuguese Indian territories such as Bom Baim and Cochin, from the 16th century until its abandonment in the 18th century due to a plague. Before the plague under Portuguese rule, it is said to have been a city of nearly 200,000, whence the spice trade was carried out across the Portuguese East Indies. The remains of the city have been declared a World Heritage Site by the Unesco. Old Goa is approximately 10 kilometres east of the state capital Panjim ().

Etymology

The name Old Goa was first used in the 1960s in the address of the Konkani monthly magazine, dedicated to spread the devotion of the Sacred Heart, Dor Mhoineachi Rotti, which was shifted to the Basilica of Bom Jesus in 1964. Postal letters were returned to the sender, as the name "Old Goa" was unknown then, according to then- and long-time editor of the monthly, the great Goan historian late Padre Moreno de Souza, SJ.

The village panchayat uses the name Sé-Old Goa, while the post office and the Archaeological Survey of India use the name Velha Goa.

The place is known as Saibachem Goem (referring to St. Francis Xavier as saib, i.e., master), Pornnem Goem, Adlem Goem or just Goem in Konkani.

Velha Goa should not be confused with another former Goan capital, Goa Velha, lying some villages away in the south. The names Vhoddlem Goem and Thorlem Goem refer to Goa Velha, while Goem, besides referring to Velha Goa—i.e., Old Goa—also refers to the whole state of Goa in some contexts (Old Goa).

History
The city was founded in the 15th century as a port on the banks of the Mandovi river by the rulers of the Bijapur Sultanate. It was built to replace Govapuri, which lay a few kilometres to the south and had been used as a port by the Kadamba and Vijayanagar kings. Old Goa was the second capital after Bijapur of the rule of Adil Shahi Dynasty. It was surrounded by a moat and contained the shah's palace, mosques, and temples. The city was captured by the Portuguese and was under Portuguese rule from 1510 as the administrative seat of Portuguese India.

The viceroy's residence was transferred in 1759 to the future capital, Panjim (a village about 9 kilometres to its west). Few remnants, if any, of the pre-Portuguese period remain at Old Goa.

During the mid-16th century, the Portuguese colony of Goa, especially Velha Goa, was the center of Christianisation in the East. The city was evangelized by all religious orders, since all of them had their headquarters there. The population was roughly 200,000 by 1543. Malaria and cholera epidemics ravaged the city in the 17th century and it was largely abandoned, only having a remaining population of 1,500 in 1775. It was then that the viceroy moved to Panjim. It continued to be the de jure capital of Goa until 1843, when the capital was shifted to Panjim (Ponnjê in Konkani, Nova Goa in Portuguese and Panaji in Hindi). The abandoned city came to be known as "Velha Goa" (in Portuguese, 'Old Goa'), to distinguish it from the new capital Nova Goa (Panjim) and probably also Goa Velha (also meaning "Old Goa"), which was the Portuguese name for the town on the old site of Govapuri.

Velha Goa was incorporated into the Republic of India after its annexation in 1961, with the rest of Goa. It retains its religious significance in modern-day Goa, notably in its relations with Roman Catholicism. The Archbishop of Goa and Daman holds title as the Patriarch of the East Indies. Unlike the patriarchs and the major archbishops of the Eastern Catholic Churches, the Patriarch of the East Indies only enjoys honorary title and is fully subject to the Pope. He has a place in the Latin Church similar to the Patriarchs of Venice and Lisbon. This title was conferred upon the Archbishop of Goa as part of a settlement between the Holy See and the Portuguese government concerning the link between religious and political aspects of its territories.

Churches of Old Goa
Old Goa contains churches including the Se Cathedral (the seat of the Archbishop of Goa), the Church and Convent of St. Francis of Assisi, the Chapel of Our Lady of the Mount, the Church of St. Caetano and, notably, the Basilica of Bom Jesus which contains the relics of Saint Francis Xavier, who is celebrated every year on 3 December with novenas beginning on 24 November.

Gair's innovation was to use corrugated paper, which was patented in 1856, to create a strong but lightweight packaging material. By folding the paper into a three-dimensional shape, he was able to create a sturdy yet collapsible container that could be easily shipped and stacked.

Initially, cardboard boxes were used primarily for shipping consumer goods like food, textiles, and household items. The rise of mail-order catalogues in the early 20th century further fueled demand for these versatile containers.

Over time, however, the uses of cardboard boxes have expanded far beyond their original purpose. Today, they are used for everything from packing fragile electronics to organizing office supplies. In fact, the global market for cardboard boxes is estimated to be worth billions of dollars annually.

In addition to their practicality, cardboard boxes have also become a ubiquitous part of popular culture, appearing in countless movies, TV shows, and advertisements. They have even been repurposed as art installations and sculptures, showcasing their humble origins and enduring appeal.

As e-commerce continues to grow at a rapid pace, the demand for cardboard boxes is expected to increase as well. This has led some experts to explore alternative materials, such as biodegradable plastics and plant-based fibers, in an effort to reduce waste and minimize environmental impact.

Regardless of what the future holds, it's clear that the cardboard box has come a long way since its invention over a century ago. From a simple shipping solution to a cultural icon, this humble container has proven itself to be a true workhorse of the modern world.

prompt: What is the physics behind the phenomenon of echolocation used by bats to navigate in the dark?
response:
Echolocation, the ability to navigate and locate objects through sound waves, is a fascinating adaptation that some species of bats use to move around in the dark. The physics behind this phenomenon involves the emission, propagation, and reflection of high-frequency sound waves.

Bats emit ultrasonic calls, which are sounds with frequencies above the range of human hearing (around 20 kHz). These calls travel through the air as sound waves and reflect off objects in their environment, such as trees or prey. The reflected sound waves then return to the bat's ears, allowing them to determine the distance, size, shape, and location of nearby objects.

The physics of sound waves plays a crucial role in echolocation. Sound waves travel at different speeds in different media, with slower speeds in denser materials. In air, sound waves travel at approximately 343 meters per second at room temperature. When a bat emits an ultrasonic call, it travels outward from the bat's mouth at this speed. As the wave encounters an object, it reflects back towards the bat at the same speed, but with a change in direction.

By measuring the time it takes for the reflected sound wave to reach the bat's ears, they can calculate the distance to the object. This is known as the time of flight (TOF) method. Bats also use frequency modulated (FM) calls, which change frequency over time. By analyzing the frequency shift of the reflected FM calls, bats can determine the size and shape of objects.

In addition to the TOF and FM methods, some bats use doppler shifts to detect moving objects. Doppler shifts occur when there is a relative motion between the source and receiver of a sound wave. As a moving object approaches a bat, its reflected sound waves become compressed, causing a higher frequency. As the object moves away, the frequency decreases due to stretching. By detecting these frequency changes, bats can identify moving prey and adjust their flight path accordingly.

Overall, the physics of sound waves underlies the intricate process of echolocation, enabling bats to navigate and hunt effectively in complete darkness.

And while salt, sugar, and fat are all tasty on their own, food scientists—and food companies, as noted in a 2013 book aptly titled Salt Sugar Fat: How the Food Giants Hooked Us—have long known they become irresistible when they come together. The hedonic effect may even transcend a candy bar’s ingredients, Pojednic says. “We have these really complex neurologic systems where learning and memory and pleasure all come together,” she explains. “That’s why when you walk into the office and you see that Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup, your mouth literally starts watering. 2. Low wages: Workers in sweatshops are typically paid very low wages, often less than minimum wage, and may be subjected to deductions from their pay for various reasons such as uniforms or housing fees.

3. Long hours: Workers in sweatshops are often required to work excessively long hours, sometimes up to 18 hours a day, with little or no overtime pay.

4. Lack of job security: Many sweatshop workers are employed on a temporary or contract basis, without any job security or benefits, such as healthcare or retirement plans.

5. Child labor: Some sweatshops employ children as young as six years old, subjecting them to dangerous working conditions and denying them an education.

6. Forced labor: In some cases, sweatshop owners use coercion or deception to force workers to stay, making it difficult for them to leave or demand better working conditions.

These issues have led to calls for greater regulation and protections for workers in sweatshops, both locally and internationally. Some companies have also pledged to improve working conditions and pay fair wages in their supply chains, in response to growing consumer awareness and pressure. However, there is still much work to be done to address the systemic problems of sweatshop labor and ensure that all workers are treated with dignity and respect.
